newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan approves taxes for stock warrant trading.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan approves taxes for stock warrant trading.

text.p: Taiwan on Saturday approved a proposal to tax stock warrant trades at between 0.1 percent and 0.3 percent, finance officials said.
"We have approved the securities authorities' proposal to tax warrant trades under the principle of taxation fairness," Finance Minister Paul Chiu announced in a news conference in Taipei.
He said such taxes are expected to become effective as soon as stock warrants are issued at the end of July or in early August.
Under the new measure, proposed by the Securities and Futures Commission, an investor must pay a transaction tax of 0.1 percent when selling a stock warrant before it is mature, Chiu said.

If an investor collects the shares on maturity of the warrant, the institution which issues the warrant must pay a 0.3 percent transaction tax, and if the investor sells the shares later, he must also pay a 0.3 percent transaction tax.
Chiu said the tax rates on warrant trades are still small compared with those of Hong Kong and Singapore.

In Hong Kong, sales of stock warrants would be charged a 0.15 percent transaction tax, while sales of the shares obtained through warrants would be imposed of a 0.3 percent transaction tax, Chiu said.
In Singapore, both tax rates are five percent, Chiu added.
In a June 2 decree issued by the ministry, securities brokerages with T$3 billion or more in registered capital are allowed to issue warrants on qualified shares.
Some 18 institutions had applied to be among the first to list warrants, which have never been allowed in Taiwan despite the relative maturity and big turnover in its stock market.
Six institutions have so far won commission approval to issue and are expected to inaugurate the issuance in late July or early August, ministry officials said.
The Taiwan Stock Exchange is managing warrant issuance under the commission's guidance and will list the instruments.
The exchange has approved 31 stock listings as qualified for inclusion in the island's debut warrants.

To qualify, a listed firm's Taiwan shares must have a total market value, based on June 30 closing prices, of more than T$25 billion, with at least 20 percent of their shares circulating in the market between January 31 to May 31, officials said.
Listed firms also must have more than 15,000 shareholders, at least 7,000 of whom must hold 1,000 to 50,000 shares.
